procedural-structure effect is an aggregation/deliberation effect that may itself be epistemically relevant.","Drug content has a single active mechanism; checklist rules may interact with procedural structure synergistically, making complete isolation artificial.","Clinical trial placebos are inert by construction; a corrupted checklist may actively mislead, creating a different baseline than mere neutrality.","The corrupted-checklist control tests content validity, but a checklist could contribute epistemically through structure alone (e.g., ensuring all relevant factors are considered), which the placebo analogy treats as non-specific."],"overturn_conditions":["The analogy breaks if checklist rules and deliberation structure are not separable in practice\u2014e.g., if panels recognize corrupted rules and disengage, making the control invalid.","The analogy fails if the procedural-structure effect is itself an epistemic good that the claim intends to capture, in which case isolating content from structure answers the wrong question.","If corrupted-checklist panels perform worse than no-checklist panels, the corruption actively harms rather than being neutral, undermining the placebo interpretation."],"shared_structure":["Both a corrupted-checklist control and a placebo control in clinical trials isolate the active ingredient from the procedural delivery mechanism.","In both cases, the treatment (checklist rules / drug content) is altered while the delivery structure (panel deliberation format / pill administration ritual) is held constant.","Both designs distinguish genuine causal efficacy of the content from non-specific effects of the procedure.","Both require that the corrupted or placebo version be indistinguishable from the real version in surface features to maintain blinding."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_007","SRC_008"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a placebo-controlled trial establishes that a drug's active ingredient causes the therapeutic effect, a corrupted-checklist control establishes that the checklist's rule content causes the reliability gain.","If a placebo produces equivalent outcomes to the active drug, the drug's content is unnecessary; analogously, if a corrupted checklist produces equivalent outcomes to the valid one, the rules are unnecessary and the gain is procedural.","The control must preserve blinding: panel members should not know whether their checklist is valid or corrupted, to prevent differential effort or engagement."]},"claim":"The proposal that non-expert panels using deliberation structure from rule content is the single-evaluation evidence that distinguishes genuine epistemic reliability gain from mere compliance artifacts.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the content.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Checklists contribute to panel performance through two orthogonal channels: (1) procedural structuring of deliberation (ensuring criteria are systematically considered, reducing omission errors), and (2) epistemic content (the rules themselves encoding domain expertise). A panel might outperform a single expert purely through the procedural channel\u2014structured discussion reduces variance and aggregates independent judgments\u2014while the checklist's rules are epiphenomenal or even incorrect. To distinguish genuine reliability gain from mere compliance, one must compare a panel using the valid checklist against a panel using a corrupted checklist that preserves procedural structure (same number of items, same deliberation flow) but contains substantively wrong rules. If both panels outperform the expert equally, the checklist's contribution is procedural, not epistemic\u2014the reliability gain is real but does not validate the checklist's content. Only if the valid-checklist panel outperforms the corrupted-checklist panel can the gain be attributed to the checklist's rules rather than to the procedural discipline of compliance. This control is necessary because without it, panel outperformance is confounded with the wisdom-of-crowds effect.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
